subject: Using SECR to inform future sampling.

messages.author: 0c0e9c17b7a87569
messages.subject: Using SECR to inform future sampling.
parts:
Hello everyone,

This is my first time posting to this forum and I'm excited to hear more about your experiences using SECR.

I'm currently a grad student in wildlife biology collecting fecal samples left behind by elk harems to estimate abundance in distinct regions throughout my study area. I haven't used SECR modeling yet however I was wondering if it can help answer a research question I have with my data. From what I've gathered, SECR is typically used to estimate density using a capture history within a home range. Has it ever been used to inform sampling protocols to anyone's knowledge?

Here's where I'm coming from: I'm using GPS data from collared elk to locate where a harem has been and where to find scat from the group (judgement sampling). These locations are based on where the elk have recently been (<week for genetic amplification reasons). I was wondering if the data I collect at these sites (# of elk identified, detecting scat, etc.) can be used to model locations or probability of detection of scat across their home range and thus inform sampling in the absence of collar data.

I appreciate any feedback you may have to this question.

Thanks.

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: Using SECR to inform future sampling.
parts:
Hi Rudy

Welcome to the group. I'm afraid SECR probably doesn't offer you much. As I understand it, you are thinking about mapping differential use within a home range.as a guide to future sampling for some other purpose. SECR tends to assume individual home ranges are circular and proceed from there to estimate population-level parameters, particularly density. The circular assumption is fairly innocuous when we  only care about population density. Technically one _can_ model irregular ranges that conform to habitat covariate(s) - see Royle, J.A., Chandler, R.B., Sun, C.C.& Fuller, A.K. (2013) Integrating resource selection information with spatial capture–recapture. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 4, 520–530 - probably a laborious and data-greedy approach to your particular problem.

I suppose even a circular home-range model might be of some use to limit a search area if you wanted to resample particular individuals, but I'm lost without a clearer idea of your mission.

Murray
